content:
Stairs can become hard during a flare, after surgery or as frailty increases. Some people move their bed downstairs for a while.

This guide explains how to plan it safely. It is educational information, not a diagnosis or personal treatment plan.

Planning the space

  • A proper bed of a suitable height, rather than a sofa.
  • Clear walkways and good lighting.
  • Keeping warm, especially overnight.
  • Privacy and dignity.

Toileting and washing

  • A commode if there is no downstairs toilet.
  • Strip washing at a sink if there is no downstairs shower.
  • Equipment such as a perching stool.

Getting help

Ask your council for an OT assessment. Short-term equipment loans may be available.

Longer-term options

  • Grab rails and a second banister.
  • A stairlift.
  • A downstairs toilet or shower, possibly through a Disabled Facilities Grant.
  • Moving to more accessible housing.

When to get help

  • Call 999 for chest pain, trouble breathing, signs of a stroke, or a fall with a possible serious injury.
  • Get urgent advice the same day (NHS 111 or your GP) for sudden confusion, a sudden drop in mobility, or a hot, swollen joint with fever.
  • See your GP for a steady decline over weeks, unplanned weight loss or repeated falls.

Never stop or change a prescribed medicine yourself. Ask your GP or pharmacist for a review.

Common questions

How long should I live downstairs?

It depends on your situation. Review it regularly with your OT.

Can I get a stairlift for free?

A Disabled Facilities Grant may help. Ask your council.

Sources and further reading

  • GOV.UK: Disabled Facilities Grants
